name: Funneling
description: Use grips and position to limit a partner’s useful choices without assuming a forced reaction. Practice one clear route and keep control when a different answer appears.
summary: Funneling means using control to make some opponent choices difficult while keeping a useful response to the choices that remain.
overview: Pick an option you want to limit, such as a guard player turning to face you. Then identify the grip, angle, or body position that actually limits it; wanting a back take does not make the opponent turn away.
key_takeaways: Name the option your control removes. A grip is useful because of what it changes.
Keep your preferred follow-up reachable from the controls you already have.
Expect more than one answer, including the opponent clearing your control or choosing not to move.
Distinguish limiting a route from provoking a reaction: a funnel shapes the available choices before you read the response.

bjj_applications.scenario: You have side control and want to follow a turn away
bjj_applications.application: Use upper-body control that limits their turn toward you. If they turn away, stay connected and work toward back control; if they remain flat, keep a suitable pin and work from there.
bjj_applications.outcome: Both staying and turning leave you with a task you have prepared.

bjj_applications.scenario: A seated guard player keeps moving away from your passing entry
bjj_applications.application: Establish a connection that lets you follow before committing your weight. Use your angle to approach one side while limiting their easy retreat.
bjj_applications.outcome: You reduce the distance they can create without treating a grip as a completed pass.

bjj_applications.scenario: A passer repeatedly circles past your unconnected feet
bjj_applications.application: Use a leg connection and an upper-body grip suited to your guard to reduce free circling. Off-balance from those connections rather than reaching after the passer with both hands.
bjj_applications.outcome: The passer must address a connection before returning to unrestricted movement.

common_mistakes.mistake: Assuming the remaining reaction is guaranteed
common_mistakes.consequence: You launch a follow-up against a response that never happened.
common_mistakes.correction: Wait for the position cue and retain an option for a partner who stays still.

common_mistakes.mistake: Removing an escape by giving up your own base
common_mistakes.consequence: The opponent reverses you while you concentrate on blocking one route.
common_mistakes.correction: Check your balance and the next likely threat whenever you change a control.

training_exercises.name: One route blocked
training_exercises.description: Start in side control. Top chooses one movement to limit: turning in or moving the hips away. Bottom tries several escapes at manageable resistance. Reset on guard recovery, reversal, a new stable pin, or a tap; compare which control actually limited the chosen route.
training_exercises.focus: Connect a control to a specific restriction.

training_exercises.name: Two acceptable outcomes
training_exercises.description: Start in butterfly guard with upper-body contact. Bottom draws the partner forward; top may stay close or withdraw. Bottom tries to off-balance a close partner or follows a withdrawal to rebuild seated contact. Reset on a sweep, pass, or lost connection.
training_exercises.focus: Prepare for the choices that remain instead of demanding one reaction.

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you know a funnel is working?
knowledge_assessment.answer: A useful opponent option becomes harder while you retain balance and a response to what they actually do.
